findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Government's decision in September 2026 to pause and review reorganisation proposals leaves the future structure of local government in Leicestershire uncertain
findings.detail: The auditor expects risks to remain once transition and implementation recommences, including the disaggregation of Council services and finances and the hosting of financial systems for the new unitary council.
findings.matters: A pause in reorganisation changes the timetable for any council that is planning for or affected by reorganisation.
findings.figures: September 2026
findings.quote: following the Government's decision in September 2026 to pause and review reorganisation proposals

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Member Code of Conduct complaints rose from 4 to 106 over the year to May 2026
findings.detail: The Council identified this as a significant governance issue in its 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement. The auditor says the Council has taken appropriate action and does not raise a formal recommendation.
findings.matters: A large increase in conduct complaints following an election is a governance signal that other councils face after May elections.
findings.quote: rising from 4 in the year to May 2025, to 106 in the year to May 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Pension Fund funding position improved from 105% at the 2022 valuation to 140% at the 31 March 2025 valuation
findings.detail: Under the funding strategy, contributions from admitted bodies funded over 120% may be reduced to let the over-funding fall gradually to 120%. The auditor records the risk register as including 19 risks.
findings.matters: A fund that has moved from 105% to 140% funded is a movement that other LGPS administering authorities will want to compare with their own valuations.
findings.quote: The Fund’s funding position has improved from 105% at the 31 March 2022 triennial valuation, to 140% at the 31 March 2025 valuation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Approved contract exceptions fell from 75 worth £7.9m in 2024/25 to 27 worth £4.0m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council attributed the reduction to enhanced scrutiny of procurement pipelines and spend data. The auditor has closed the 2023/24 recommendation on contract exceptions.
findings.matters: A fall in contract exceptions, with a recommendation closed on the basis of it, is a control result peers can compare against their own procurement compliance.
findings.quote: reported a reduction in approved exceptions from 75, with a value of £7.9m in 2024/25 to 27 with a value of £4.0m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Internal Audit delivered 816 audit days against a planned 1,140 days (71.6%) in 2025/26
findings.detail: The shortfall was primarily due to vacancies within the Internal Audit team. The auditor has raised an insight on resourcing the function.
findings.matters: Internal audit capacity is a resource question many councils face, and the plan delivery figure is directly comparable.
findings.figures: 816 audit days; 1,140 days; 71.6%
findings.quote: delivery of the Internal Audit plan was below the level originally planned for 2025/26, with 816 audit days delivered against a planned 1,140 days (71.6%).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Audit raises 8 recommendations this year, with 6 from the prior year not yet actioned
findings.detail: The auditor also reports one non-material adjustment, where assets from previous academy schools were omitted from the balance sheet. The auditor raised an improvement recommendation on the timeliness and accuracy of working papers for the accounts.
findings.matters: A growing count of open audit recommendations is an operational finding peers and lenders can compare against their own audit record.
findings.figures: 8 recommendations; 6 prior-year recommendations
findings.quote: We have raised 8 recommendations as part of the audit this year, and there remain 6 from the prior year that have not yet been actioned.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Council provided draft accounts by the national deadline of 30 June 2026, and the auditor intends to issue an unqualified opinion
findings.detail: The draft accounts were of reasonable standard, with two exceptions in relation to the land and buildings valuation process and receivable and payable breakdowns. The audit opinion will follow the Corporate Governance Committee meeting on 27 November 2026.
findings.matters: Meeting the 30 June draft deadline and expecting an unqualified opinion are facts other councils use to benchmark their own closedown and audit timetable.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026; 27 November 2026
findings.quote: We have substantially completed our audit of your financial statements and intend to issue an unqualified audit opinion

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves of £257m at year end, including £90.4m within the budget equalisation reserve
findings.detail: The auditor says this provides sufficient cover for planned use of reserves in 2026/27 and the currently forecast funding gap in 2027/28. The auditor also notes the Council recognises reliance on reserves is not sustainable long-term.
findings.matters: The size of the budget equalisation reserve against the forecast gap is the key number for any council drawing on reserves to balance its budget.
findings.quote: The Council also held £257m of earmarked reserves at year end, including £90.4m within the budget equalisation reserve, providing sufficient cover for the planned use of reserves in 2026/27 and the currently forecast funding gap in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: General Fund balance at £26m at 31 March 2026, 4.2% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget
findings.detail: The balance is within the Council's target range of 4% to 7% of net expenditure, but towards the lower end. The Council plans to increase it by £1m each year across the MTFS.
findings.matters: A general fund balance near the bottom of a reserves policy range is a figure that peers and lenders benchmark against target ranges.
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the General Fund balance stood at £26m, equivalent to 4.2% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget and therefore within the Council's target range, albeit towards the lower end.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Capital programme of £501m to 2029/30 has a funding gap of £75.0m
findings.detail: The programme is funded through grants (£273.5m), capital receipts (£23.1m), revenue and reserves (£83.0m) and external contributions (£46.3m). The paper says the capital programme includes over £70m of transport investment in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A capital programme with an unfunded gap of this size is a capital risk that finance directors and lenders will want to track.
findings.quote: The draft capital programme totals £501m to 2029/30 and is funded through grants (£273.5m), capital receipts (£23.1m), revenue and reserves (£83.0m) and external contributions (£46.3m), leaving a funding gap of £75.0m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: External borrowing at £130m, the lowest level for 20 years, following a policy of repaying debt
findings.detail: The Council's cost of financing relative to its net revenue stream is 2.6%, which the auditor describes as low relative to comparable councils. The capital programme is planned at £501m over four years.
findings.matters: A council reducing external borrowing to a 20-year low is a borrowing position that lenders and treasury teams will want to see.
findings.quote: The Council reported that its overall level of external borrowing, at £130m, was at the lowest level for 20 years following a policy of repaying debt.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Children’s and Families Department overspent by £2.6m in 2025/26, mainly on Children’s Social Care Placements
findings.detail: The overspend was offset by net underspends of £5.7m in Environment and Transport and £3.9m in Adults and Communities, mainly from higher-income vacancies.
findings.matters: Children's social care placement costs are the demand pressure that other councils report most often, and this figure is the directorate-level outturn.
findings.quote: a £2.6m overspend for Children’s and Families Department was reported driven mainly by Children’s Social Care Placements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Council reports a balanced 2025/26 outturn after a £7m revenue underspend, set aside for debt repayment, highways and efficiency
findings.detail: The underspend was set aside as £2.5m for debt repayment, £2.5m for the Highways Investment Fund and £2.0m for the Council's Efficiency Review. The auditor notes that vacancies are not recurrent savings.
findings.matters: A balanced outturn with the underspend ring-fenced to specific uses is a reportable position for peers managing similar demand pressures.
findings.quote: The Council reported an overall balanced outturn position for 2025/26, after a revenue underspend of £7m, which was set aside for Debt Repayment (£2.5m), the Highways Investment Fund (£2.5m) and the Council’s Efficiency Review (£2.0m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Auditor raises an improvement recommendation on monitoring and delivery of savings plans
findings.detail: The auditor says Cabinet has limited routine reporting on savings progress. The Council says formal progress reporting of the Better Leicestershire Programme to Cabinet and Scrutiny is being put in place, with the first update due in November.
findings.matters: Savings delivery reporting is an open question at many councils, and this is a formal external finding on it.
findings.quote: Given the strategic importance of delivering its planned savings, including through the Better Leicestershire Programme and the significant investment required, the Council should strengthen arrangements for monitoring and reporting progress.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Efficiency Review identified estimated savings of £27m over the MTFS period, with potential of up to £60m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The review was commissioned in November 2025. Its findings have been incorporated into the Better Leicestershire Programme, for which the Cabinet approved an investment fund of up to £20m in May 2026.
findings.matters: A quantified saving estimate set against a rising funding gap is the figure a lender or peer council would want to test against delivery.
findings.quote: The outcome of the review identified estimated savings of £27m over the MTFS period and the potential to generate up to £60m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget requires £15.4m from the Budget Equalisation Reserve, with MTFS funding gaps rising to £84.5m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The MTFS shows funding gaps rising from £34.2m in 2027/28. The auditor says the Council continues to face significant forecast funding gaps.
findings.matters: Reliance on a reserve to balance the budget, alongside a rising MTFS gap, is the situation a finance director at another council would compare their own plan against.
findings.quote: However, setting a balanced budget required a £15.4m contribution from the Council’s budget equalisation reserve, and the MTFS forecasts funding gaps increasing from £34.2m in 2027/28 to £84.5m by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Auditor retains a key recommendation on the DSG deficit, with a significant weakness identified for 2025/26
findings.detail: The auditor found a significant weakness in arrangements in relation to the DSG deficit for 2025/26. The key recommendation from 2024/25 has been updated and carried forward.
findings.matters: A key recommendation on DSG governance from external audit is a public, formal finding that other councils with DSG deficits will be compared against.
findings.quote: We have therefore retained and updated the prior year key recommendation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant supported the DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 by £71.3m
findings.detail: The paper records the grant as supporting the deficit as at 31 March 2026. It also says further work is required to mitigate continued growth of the deficit.
findings.matters: The size of the grant contribution is the figure a finance director needs to compare against the gross deficit when assessing their own exposure.
findings.quote: The High Needs Stability Grant has supported the DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026 by £71.3m; however, further work is required to mitigate the continued growth of the deficit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: £32m earmarked within the Budget Equalisation Reserve for the net High Needs element of the DSG deficit
findings.detail: The auditor considers this provision sufficient to cover the currently estimated share of the deficit accrued to 31 March 2026, and describes this as positive.
findings.matters: Showing how a residual DSG liability is funded from reserves is a question other councils facing the same government support structure will need to answer.
findings.quote: The Council has earmarked £32m within the Budget Equalisation Reserve to fund the net deficit on the High Needs element of the DSG.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Council received confirmation in October 2026 that it will receive funding equivalent to 90% of the accumulated DSG deficit at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The Council submitted its SEND Reform Plan by the national deadline of 19 June 2026. The Council had previously estimated a residual liability of around £30m on the net forecast deficit of £94m.
findings.matters: Government support covering 90% of the accumulated deficit determines how much of the DSG deficit falls on council reserves, which is relevant to every council with a DSG deficit.
findings.quote: received confirmation in October 2026 that it will receive funding equivalent to 90% of the accumulated DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026 and has earmarked reserves

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Council forecasts the cumulative DSG deficit could exceed £400m by March 2030 without significant reform
findings.detail: The Council's own forecast is that the deficit keeps growing without reform. The auditor says the extent of government support beyond 2025/26 remains uncertain.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would want to see the size of the forecast tail risk if national reform is not delivered.
findings.figures: £400m; March 2030
findings.quote: The Council forecast that, without significant reform, the cumulative DSG deficit could exceed £400m by March 2030.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC AAR 2025-26 - 171126
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit rose by £30.9m (64%) to £79.2m at 31 March 2026, from £48.3m a year earlier
findings.detail: The increase was driven by a £34.7m overspend on the High Needs Block, partly offset by underspends of £2.9m on the Early Years Block and £0.9m on the Schools Block. The cumulative High Needs deficit rose from £64.4m to £99.1m over the same year.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a DSG deficit can compare the size and growth rate of this deficit against their own High Needs position.
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the cumulative DSG deficit increased by £30.9m (64%) to £79.2m (2024/25: £48.3m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The paper reports the 2025/26 Fair Funding settlement, covering 2026/27 to 2028/29, as having 'a limited impact' on the council's financial position.
findings.detail: The paper says the settlement includes some improvements but diverts funding to urban councils. It states that county areas saw the biggest increases in needs.
findings.matters: Changes in the funding formula affect how much each council receives, and peer councils compare their settlements against this assessment.
findings.figures: Settlement period 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: The new settlement has had a limited impact on the Council’s financial position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: Pension Fund net assets were reported at £7,502.3m at 31 March 2026, up from £6,697.6m a year earlier.
findings.detail: The Fund account shows a net increase in net assets for the year, and the investment returns line shows £683.0m of profits and changes in value. Employer contributions were £259.0m.
findings.matters: Pension Fund net assets and the scale of investment gains are the measures actuaries and other funds use to assess funding positions.
findings.figures: Net assets £7,502.3m (£6,697.6m at 31 March 2025); net returns on investments £780.1m; employer contributions £259.0m
findings.quote: Net Assets of the Fund at 31 March

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The Annual Governance Statement reports two governance issues that the paper describes as significant for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the statement finds the council has effective governance arrangements but needs to keep reviewing them. The detail on the two issues is in section 8 of the AGS.
findings.matters: Governance issues flagged in the annual statement are the items external auditors and peers look at first.
findings.figures: 2 significant governance issues
findings.quote: There were 2 significant governance issues in 2025/26 which are further explained in section 8 of the AGS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The accounts were authorised for issue on 27 November 2026 as unaudited.
findings.detail: The paper states the accounts are unaudited at authorisation, and the contents list the audit opinion as 'To Follow'. The paper does not report an audit outcome.
findings.matters: A council whose audit opinion is still to come is one a lender or peer would track until the opinion is published.
findings.figures: Authorised 27 November 2026; audit opinion to follow
findings.quote: The unaudited accounts were authorised for issue on 27 November 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The council says it does not anticipate needing to issue a Section 114 notice in 2026/27, while future years remain uncertain.
findings.detail: The paper links the uncertainty to ongoing demand pressures, the outcome of Local Government Reorganisation and further government reforms. It says the position will be reviewed each year.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is the formal sign of a council unable to balance its budget, and both peers and lenders monitor whether a council states it will not need one.
findings.figures: None in the sentence; the notice is not anticipated for 2026/27
findings.quote: the Authority does not anticipate that it will need to issue a Section 114 notice (Local Government Finance Act 1988) in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The government withdrew its July 2026 decision to reorganise Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland into two new unitary councils from April 2028.
findings.detail: The paper says the government is reviewing LGR and will undertake a further review of options for the areas where decisions were withdrawn, with information to be provided by early next year.
findings.matters: A withdrawn reorganisation decision leaves the council's future structure and its budget planning uncertain, which other councils in restructuring areas will also face.
findings.figures: Decision announced July 2026; withdrawn October 2026; new unitary councils had been due from April 2028
findings.quote: in October 2026 they withdrew their July 2026 decision for Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The council has set aside £12m in an earmarked reserve to contribute to the costs of Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS for 2026-30 was based on a neutral position while the government decision was awaited, so the reserve is the council's own provision for LGR costs.
findings.matters: A council ring-fencing reserves for reorganisation costs is a common step, and the amount is a benchmark for peers facing the same process.
findings.figures: £12m earmarked reserve for LGR costs
findings.quote: The Council has however set aside £12m in an earmarked reserve to contribute to the costs of LGR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: Government approved the council's SEND reform plan in October 2026 and awarded a grant of 90% of the deficit.
findings.detail: The paper says the support relates to deficits as at 31 March 2026, and that details for deficits after that date remain uncertain. Government announced in February 2026 that it would support councils with DSG deficits.
findings.matters: A government grant covering most of an accumulated DSG deficit changes the funding position other councils with similar deficits are waiting on.
findings.figures: Grant of 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: In October 2026 the Government approved the Authority’s SEND reform plan and awarded the Authority a grant of 90% of the deficit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The council reports a DSG deficit of £79m at 31 March 2026, which it forecasts will exceed £400m by 2030.
findings.detail: The paper links the forecast to SEND pressures and says the DfE's plans for SEND spending after April 2028 are uncertain. It says the MTFS includes £66m of savings within the High Needs DSG.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit growing toward £400m is a large unfunded liability that other councils and lenders would weigh against reserves.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £79m at 31 March 2026; forecast above £400m by 2030; £66m planned SEND savings within the DSG
findings.quote: At year end, 31 March 2026, the Council had a DSG deficit of £79m which is forecast to exceed £400m by 2030.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: External debt fell to £131m at 31 March 2026 from £175m, and no new external loans were raised in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the gap between the Capital Financing Requirement and actual debt is temporarily funded by internal borrowing from investment balances. It says the level of borrowing is within the 2025/26 prudential indicators.
findings.matters: A council using internal borrowing and reducing external debt changes its exposure to refinancing and interest rate risk, which is what a lender assesses.
findings.figures: Actual debt £131m (£175m, 31 March 2025); CFR £193m (£198m, 31 March 2025); no new external loans (£0m 2024/25); investments £387m (£410m, 31 March 2025)
findings.quote: actual debt was £131m as at 31 March 2026 (£175m, 31 March 2025)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The council states that £140m of 2025/26 capital investment was funded without any new borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper lists £31m for Children and Family Services, including 1,625 additional school places, £35m for highways asset maintenance and £48m on major infrastructure projects.
findings.matters: Capital delivered without new borrowing is a funding choice that a lender and a peer council would each read differently.
findings.figures: £140m capital investment; £31m Children and Family Services; £35m highways asset maintenance; £48m major infrastructure
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council invested £140m in a number of capital projects, all funded without the need for any new borrowing

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The 2025/26 capital outturn was £140.2m against a £205.4m budget, with a £65.2m variance carried into the 2026-30 capital programme.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the variance to rephasing of expenditure on projects. Environment and Transport accounted for the largest variance at £36.5m, and Children and Family Services at £20.9m.
findings.matters: Large capital rephasing shows delivery pressure, and a finance director at another council compares how much of a programme slips into later years.
findings.figures: Capital budget £205.4m; outturn £140.2m; variance £65.2m; Environment & Transport variance £36.5m; Children & Family Services variance £20.9m
findings.quote: Overall, there has been a net variance of £65m compared with the updated budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The 2026-30 MTFS identifies £115m of savings still to be delivered by 2029/30, against a funding gap rising from £36m in 2027/28 to £85m by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has saved £290m since 2010. It describes the funding gap as an estimate and states that the savings requirement sits alongside the MTFS plan.
findings.matters: A savings target that grows against a funding gap is the core test of a medium-term plan, and lenders and peers compare the scale of the remaining gap.
findings.figures: £115m identified savings to be delivered by 2029/30; funding gap £36m in 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30; £290m saved since 2010
findings.quote: as well as closing an estimated funding gap of £36m in 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: Children and Family Services overspent its 2025/26 revenue budget, with the paper citing cost and demand pressures on social care and special educational needs.
findings.detail: The paper says the year saw increasing cost and demand pressures on Children’s social care services and special educational needs. The budget and outturn table records the overspend on that line.
findings.matters: Children's social care and SEND demand is the pressure most councils report, so the size of the overspend is a useful comparator for peers.
findings.figures: Budget £145.4m; outturn £148.0m; overspend £2.6m
findings.quote: The financial year saw additional increasing cost and demand pressures on Children’s social care services and special educational needs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: Environment and Transport reported a £5.7m net underspend, with over half of it from the early achievement of savings.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the balance of the underspend to additional income and recruitment challenges. It also says a review will check whether reductions can be made to the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Savings delivered ahead of plan are a direct input to the funding gap, and a finance director at another council can compare the scale of early delivery.
findings.figures: Budget £123.2m; outturn £117.4m; underspend £5.7m
findings.quote: Environment and Transport had a net underspend of £5.7m, over half of which related to the early achievement of savings

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 2025-26 Final Statement Of Accounts, Annual Governance Statement And Pension Fund Accounts
findings.headline: The 2025/26 net revenue outturn was reported as balanced, with £615.0m spent against a £615.4m budget after £7.0m was set aside for additional commitments.
findings.detail: The paper says the outturn was balanced after £7.0m was set aside for debt repayment (£2.5m), the highways investment fund (£2.5m) and the efficiency review (£2.0m). Children and Family Services overspent while Adults and Communities and Environment and Transport underspent.
findings.matters: A council that balances its revenue outturn by earmarking underspends for later commitments shows how its 2026/27 budget review will be shaped, which peers and lenders track.
findings.figures: Budget £615.4m; outturn £615.0m; variance £0.3m favourable; £7.0m set aside for additional commitments
findings.quote: The 2025/26 net outturn showed a balanced position, after funding of £7.0m was set aside for additional commitments

findings.paper_title: Revised Audit Committee Guidance
findings.headline: The Head of Internal Audit reports Leicestershire's current audit committee arrangements as satisfactory against CIPFA's 2026 Position Statement, with a few gaps identified in Appendix 2.
findings.detail: The paper says the Head of Internal Audit Service reviewed current arrangements against the 2026 Position Statement and found them satisfactory, identifying a few gaps. The gaps are listed in Appendix 2, which is referenced but not included in the text provided. The paper also proposes a self-assessment using CIPFA's five-level maturity model, to be undertaken annually in late spring.
findings.matters: Peer finance officers preparing for the new statutory duty and the 2026 Position Statement will want to compare their own gap assessments and self-assessment approach.
findings.figures: Five maturity levels: initial; developing; established; advanced and leading practice
findings.quote: found them to be satisfactory and has only identified a few gaps

findings.paper_title: Revised Audit Committee Guidance
findings.headline: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 makes an audit committee a statutory requirement for most English local authorities, with at least one independent member.
findings.detail: The paper says Section 94 of the Act inserted a new section 33A into the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014, requiring a relevant authority other than a health service body to have an audit committee. The audit committee must review financial affairs, risk management, internal control and governance, value for money, and make reports and recommendations. Authorities must also have at least one independent member.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council needs to know that audit committees have moved from good practice to a legal duty, with specified functions and an independent member requirement.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Act introduced a new statutory requirement for most local authorities in England to have an audit committee.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - LCC Pension Fund AFR 2025-26
findings.headline: Auditor recommends that the financial statements explain the current position on the Virgin Media case.
findings.detail: The auditor lists this as a disclosure change to be made, and management has agreed. The paper does not describe the case or any financial effect.
findings.matters: The Virgin Media case concerns the treatment of LGPS benefits and has been reported across the sector, so funds will be checking how peers disclose its current position.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: Disclosures to explain the current position in relation to Virgin Media case should be included within the financial statements.

findings.headline: Annual pension statements not issued to 9 members at two employers due to unresolved admission agreements
findings.detail: While most annual pension statements were produced by the 31 August 2026 statutory deadline (38,553 active member and 32,074 deferred member statements), two employers' employees did not receive statements due to outstanding admission agreement issues. 9 scheme members were affected. At time of writing, the admission agreements remained unresolved and statements have not yet been produced.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver statutory pension communications to eligible members indicates governance capacity issues affecting member protections and statutory compliance.
findings.figures: 9 members affected; 2 employers involved; 38,553 active and 32,074 deferred statements issued overall
findings.quote: There were two employers where their employees did not receive statements due to issues related to employer admission agreements. The employees have been notified in writing of the position and statements. In total, 9 scheme members were affected by this. At the time of writing, the admission agreements remained outstanding and the statements have not yet been produced.

findings.paper_title: LOCAL PENSION BOARD - Admin Report Quarter Two
findings.headline: McCloud remedy retrospective adjustments not completed by 31 August 2026 statutory deadline
findings.detail: The council missed the statutory deadline for completing McCloud adjustments to pension records. While not deemed a material breach, the Pensions Manager reported this to the Pensions Regulator on 25 August 2026 with a revised completion date of 31 December 2026. 19 transfer cases remained outstanding at time of writing.
findings.matters: A council missing statutory deadlines and self-reporting to regulators suggests governance capacity issues that could extend to other regulated functions.
findings.figures: 31 August 2026 (missed deadline); 31 December 2026 (revised deadline); 19 transfer cases outstanding
findings.quote: The retrospective adjustments to pension records generated by the remedy were not completed by the stated deadline of 31 August 2026. Whilst this is not deemed a material breach of law, the Pensions Manager reported the position to The Pensions Regulator on 25 August 2026 with a revised date for completion of 31 December 2026.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Pooled property fund investments are now valued below invested capital, showing unrealised losses of approximately £1.4m.
findings.detail: Two UK commercial pooled property funds committed between 2015 and 2019 (Threadneedle and DTZ managed active value) now have NAV of £7.6m against capital invested of £9m. Council attributes below-cost valuations to higher interest rates and changed property market conditions compared to very low rate environment when originally invested. Threadneedle (open-ended) can be held indefinitely; DTZ (closed-ended) is returning capital as properties are sold.
findings.matters: Demonstrates value destruction in strategic property investments from interest rate and market movements; shows impact of higher rate environment on fixed-asset valuations.
findings.figures: £9m capital invested; £7.6m current NAV; ~£1.4m unrealised loss; 2.2% IRR since inception
findings.quote: Both pooled property funds have current valuations below the invested capital. This is generally due to the higher value of property when these investments were originally made (during a very low UK interest rate period) compared to the valuations in a higher UK interest rate environment.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Council is £102m underborrowed against Capital Financing Requirement, managing position through £335m investment balances.
findings.detail: With external debt of £87m against estimated CFR of £189m, council has substantial underborrowing position. Rather than accessing external borrowing markets, manages longer-term cash through investment balances of £335m. This demonstrates strong liquidity and financial capacity but indicates council has not needed to access markets recently and may have over-accumulated cash reserves.
findings.matters: Underborrowed position and reliance on internal investment reserves indicate strong balance sheet and borrowing capacity; relevant to understanding council's future refinancing needs and market access profile.
findings.figures: £87m external debt; £189m estimated CFR; £102m underborrowed; £335m investment balances
findings.quote: Comparing the actual external debt to the CFR, the Council is forecast to be £102m underborrowed at year end. With investment balances of £335m, this position can be managed using internal investment balances rather than more expensive external borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Financing costs exceeded prudential indicator by 0.1% due to premiums paid on early debt repayment.
findings.detail: Council exceeded prudential indicator for actual financing costs as percentage of net revenue stream by 0.1%, directly attributable to £8.2m premiums paid on early PWLB repayments. Council states this was exception to normal prudential adherence, driven by deliberate debt repayment strategy. Excess is immaterial but represents trade-off between prudential compliance and debt reduction objective.
findings.matters: Shows council chose to exceed its own prudential limits in pursuit of debt reduction strategy; indicates financial costs of early repayment were higher than originally budgeted.
findings.figures: 0.1% excess on financing costs as percentage of net revenue stream; £8.2m premiums paid on early repayments
findings.quote: The Council has operated within the treasury and prudential indicators... except for the actual financing costs as a % of net revenue stream by 0.1% due to the premiums payable on the early repayment of debt.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast for 2026-27 increased by £17m to £181m after MTFS approval, driven by additional government grants and rephasing.
findings.detail: Original prudential indicator set at £164m; forecast now £181m due to additional government capital grants announced after February 2026 MTFS approval and rephasing of expenditure from 2025/26 outturn. Council confirms the increase is fully funded and represents post-approval change to capital strategy, signalling either improved funding availability or rescheduling of investment schemes.
findings.matters: Material increase in capital expenditure signals either improved funding availability or rephasing of investment schemes, with implications for borrowing requirements and the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.figures: £181m forecast vs £164m prudential indicator; £17m increase
findings.quote: The latest estimate of capital expenditure in 2026/27 is £181m compared with the original prudential indicator of £164m. The increase is due to additional government capital grants, announced after the MTFS was approved, and the rephasing of capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Two LOBO loans totalling £20m were called by FMS and Dexia with lender options to increase rates; council repaid at par without premiums.
findings.detail: FMS loan of £10m at 4.75% coupon (maturity 2054) and Dexia loan of £10m at 4.50% coupon (maturity 2065) were subject to lender call options exercised to increase rates to significantly higher levels. Council chose to repay at par with no redemption premiums rather than accept the higher rates. This eliminates long-dated, high-legacy-cost liabilities and represents a lender-initiated refinancing and liquidity event.
findings.matters: Lender exercise of LOBO call options is a refinancing and liquidity event that extinguishes exposure to significantly higher rates on legacy loans and removes interest rate risk.
findings.figures: FMS: £10m at 4.75%, maturity 2054; Dexia: £10m at 4.50%, maturity 2065; zero premiums on LOBO repayments
findings.quote: The lender exercised their call option to change the interest rates on the loans (to a significantly higher rate). As a result, the Council took the opportunity to repay these loans, no premiums apply in these circumstances.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly TM Report Q1 26-27 Final
findings.headline: Council repaid £42.7m of external debt in Q1 2026-27, reducing total debt to £87m - the lowest level in over 30 years.
findings.detail: Debt repayment included £20m in LOBO loans with no premiums, plus £22.7m in PWLB loans with £8.2m premiums paid. Council projects annual interest savings of £2.8m, with estimated net annual cash saving of £1.1m after accounting for foregone investment income. This represents the most significant debt reduction in decades and strengthens the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Demonstrates major improvement in financial position and reduced debt service obligations, lowering financial risk and improving fiscal sustainability.
findings.figures: £42.7m repaid; £87m remaining external debt (lowest in 30 years); £2.8m annual interest savings; £1.1m net annual cash saving after foregone investment income
findings.quote: The Council has repaid a total of £42.7m of external debt principal in the current financial year to date. The Council's actual level of external debt now stands at £87m, the lowest level for over 30 years.

findings.paper_title: Insurance Service Annual Report 2025-26 - final to CGC
findings.headline: Current insurance arrangements enter break clause period from October 2027, allowing either party to exit or renegotiate
findings.detail: The council's insurance programme was tendered in 2024 on a 3+2+2+2 basis. The insurance year October 2026–September 2027 is the last year of the current agreement. After September 2027, either the council or its insurers can trigger break clauses.
findings.matters: Insurance arrangements are about to enter a period where either party can force renegotiation or exit, creating potential for cover disruption, rate spikes, or need to secure alternative arrangements.
findings.figures: Current agreement: 3+2+2+2 basis; break clauses available from October 2027
findings.quote: The forthcoming insurance year (October 2026 to September 2027) is the last before the Council or the insurer can trigger break clauses should they be necessary.

findings.paper_title: Insurance Service Annual Report 2025-26 - final to CGC
findings.headline: Insurance gap where academy trusts do construction on council property identified but unresolved
findings.detail: The Insurance Service identified potential risk exposure where academy trusts undertake construction and capital works on council-owned property. Work is underway to ensure adequate insurance arrangements, but this remains ongoing and unresolved.
findings.matters: An unresolved insurance gap could expose the council to uninsured losses if academy construction projects result in damage, defects, or liability claims.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Service has identified and commenced work on a potential risk exposure associated with construction and capital works being undertaken by Academy Trusts on Leicestershire County Council -owned properties.

findings.paper_title: Insurance Service Annual Report 2025-26 - final to CGC
findings.headline: New risk-based highway inspection approach (1 July 2026) explicitly risks worsening claims performance if repair times increase
findings.detail: Immediately following Q4 2025 claims problems driven by inspection delays and missed repairs, the council implemented a new risk-based approach to highway inspection. The Insurance Service explicitly flags that any increase in repair times under the new model could damage claims performance, creating risk that this operational change amplifies the problems it follows.
findings.matters: A recent operational change to highways management creates direct risk that insurance costs and claim exposure will increase if defects are repaired more slowly.
findings.figures: New approach effective 1 July 2026
findings.quote: Any significant increase in repair times, could impact the Insurance Service claims performance.

findings.paper_title: Insurance Service Annual Report 2025-26 - final to CGC
findings.headline: Employer liability claims rose 79% in three years to £316k; Q4 repudiation rate fell to 60% against 87% target due to missed inspections and delayed repairs
findings.detail: Liability claims rose from £176k (2023-24) to £316k (2025-26). In Q4 2025, missed highway inspections and delays in completing repairs within policy timeframes forced the council to pay claims that would normally be repudiated, dropping the repudiation rate to 60% against an 87% target. This suggests operational failures are creating material financial exposure.
findings.matters: Operational failings in highway maintenance are increasing self-insured claim payouts, indicating service deterioration or cost pressures that reduce the council's ability to defend claims.
findings.figures: Liability claims: £176k (2023-24), £262k (2024-25), £316k (2025-26); Q4 repudiation rate 60% vs 87% target
findings.quote: In Q4 there was an increase in the number of pothole claims received, due to prolonged poor weather and deterioration of the network , missed highways inspections and repairs were not completed within policy timeframes.

findings.paper_title: Insurance Service Annual Report 2025-26 - final to CGC
findings.headline: MMI contingent levy at 25% could rise if asbestos and abuse claims exceed actuarial assumptions
findings.detail: The council is self-insured for 25% of Municipal Mutual Insurance claims following scheme levies triggered in 2012. The scheme administrator's actuaries cannot guarantee this percentage will remain sufficient. Increasing treatment costs for asbestos claims, legislative and court changes affecting abuse claims, and claims expected to run until 2060 create downside risk to the levy.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could crystallize and require additional financial provision if claims trends worsen beyond current actuarial models.
findings.figures: 25% self-insured levy; MMI run-off expected until 2060
findings.quote: Due to the latent nature of some claims, MMI's independent actuaries (KPMG) projections are subject to substantial uncertainty , and it is not possible to guarantee that the total levy percentage of 25% will remain sufficient

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: East Midlands Gateway 2 development proceeding with no agreed highway and transport mitigation for local road network
findings.detail: The East Midlands Gateway Development Consent Order application entered examination in March 2026. The council has made submissions to the examination and participated in hearings, raising specific concerns about predicted traffic increases through Kegworth and Castle Donington. However, there is currently no agreed scheme of highway and transport mitigation with the applicant, and the applicant has made no commitment to address the council's concerns.
findings.matters: Lack of agreed infrastructure mitigation creates risk that development proceeds without compensating investment in council services, potentially imposing unbudgeted costs on the authority and impeding delivery of Local Plan growth.
findings.figures: No specific traffic impact quantification provided
findings.quote: Whilst Officers continue to work with the Applicant to resolve outstanding matters of concern, there is currently no agreed scheme of highway and transport mitigation for the Local Road Network, and to date no commitment from the Applicant to address.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: Waste service experienced operational strain with temporary closure of four recycling sites in August
findings.detail: Four Recycling and Household Waste Sites were temporarily closed from early August 2026 due to very high demand combined with staff shortages (driver vacancies, sickness, planned leave), delays at treatment facilities and plant breakdowns. Planned waste transfer station works scheduled for 2026/27 are expected to reduce risk once completed. Demand is being driven in part by food waste transfers from district council collections.
findings.matters: Service disruption signals underlying operational strain from demand exceeding available capacity and staffing. Recovery depends on capital works (transfer station) completing on schedule in 2026/27.
findings.figures: 4 Recycling and Household Waste Sites temporarily closed from early August
findings.quote: Very high demand across the Recycling and Household Waste Site service coupled with staff shortages (driver shortages, sickness, planned leave and vacancies), delays / availability at treatment facilities and plant break downs led to the temporary closure of 4 RHWS from early August.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: 518 children and young people awaiting specialist school places; SEND service capacity overwhelmed
findings.detail: The SEND service has 518 children and young people currently awaiting specialist school places within Leicestershire. The shortfall in registered specialist provision has increased demand on Oakfield Short Stay School beyond sustainable levels. A new 252-place special school for the South of the County is planned for 2028 delivery, alongside additional places at existing schools, but significant lag in provision remains.
findings.matters: Large unmet demand for SEND places creates statutory compliance risk, long waiting lists, pressure on interim provision, and potential breach of parental rights to appropriate provision.
findings.figures: 518 children and young people awaiting specialist school places
findings.quote: There are currently 518 children and young people awaiting specialist school places within Leicestershire.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: Children & Family Services faces significant recruitment and retention difficulty with widening gaps in agency labour market
findings.detail: Children & Family Services faces significant difficulty recruiting and retaining permanent staff, with widening gaps in the agency labour market making it impossible to source sufficient quality agency workers to fill vacancies. The assessment explicitly flags crisis potential. Local Government Reorganisation is expected to compound recruitment and retention pressures further.
findings.matters: Workforce shortages force reliance on expensive agency staff (creating budget overspend risk), impair service delivery for vulnerable children, and create service continuity risk. LGR uncertainty compounds instability.
findings.figures: No quantification of current vacant posts or agency cost impact disclosed
findings.quote: we are seeing increasing gaps in the agency market which means that gaps in our permanent workforce are difficult to fill with the quality of agency that we need to undertake - this does appear to have the potential to move us into a period of crisis if not managed well.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: External efficiency review identifies £27m in savings across MTFS period, but delivery remains unproven and £60m stretch target implies gap
findings.detail: An external efficiency review completed in May 2026 identified potential savings of £27m across the Medium Term Financial Strategy period, with a stretch target approaching £60m. The Cabinet approved a revised Transformation Programme and mobilisation is now underway. Separately, Adult and Community Services forecasts showed a £230k overspend in period 3, and income targets for cultural services (including £80k uplift from Country Parks fees) are being monitored.
findings.matters: Significant savings are needed to balance the budget, but the gap between identified (£27m) and stretch target (£60m) represents material delivery risk, and early-period overspends signal that cost control remains challenging.
findings.figures: £27m identified, £60m stretch target, £230k A&CS period 3 overspend, £80k Country Parks income uplift
findings.quote: The review is now complete and identified potential savings of £27m across the MTFS period, with a stretch target approaching £60m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: £100m+ capital shortfall for 17 new mainstream schools remains unresolved
findings.detail: The council faces a capital shortfall of over £100m needed to deliver 17 new mainstream schools required to meet Special Educational Needs demand. Mitigation measures including standardised designs, value engineering, phased delivery and planning obligations policy refresh are underway, but the gap remains substantial.
findings.matters: A major unresolved capital gap creates risk that the council cannot meet statutory place planning requirements and may fail to deliver SEND compliance, with potential legal and service delivery consequences.
findings.figures: Over £100m shortfall for 17 new mainstream schools
findings.quote: A capital shortfall of over £100m for 17 new mainstream schools continues to be a significant concern.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Risk Register (July August 2026)
findings.headline: Government confirms backing of 90% of historic Special Educational Needs deficits, but payment timing and detail remain unclear
findings.detail: The council has received confirmation that government will fund 90% of accumulated high needs block deficits accumulated up to 31 March 2026. However, the specific details of the funding mechanism and the timeframe for payment have not yet been confirmed. Further announcements are expected in the Autumn.
findings.matters: Government backing eliminates most of a known historic liability, materially improving the council's financial position, but timing uncertainty creates budget planning risk.
findings.figures: 90% of accumulated deficits up to 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Confirmation hs been received that the Government will pay up to 90% of deficits accumulated up to 31 March 2026. However, the detail and timeframe as yet to be confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Risks Removed
findings.headline: Inflation has stabilised and corporate cost of living crisis risk downscaled to departmental management level
findings.detail: The corporate cost of living crisis risk has been downscaled as inflation has stabilised. However, the paper notes that wider impacts remain embedded in the medium-term financial strategy and children's services corporate risks, now managed at department level.
findings.matters: Inflation and cost of living pressures directly impact council finances; stabilisation suggests some budget pressure relief, though residual impacts persist within the financial strategy
findings.figures: No specific financial figures provided in the paper
findings.quote: Inflation has stabilised and whilst there are still wider impacts ingrained within the MTFS and Children's services corporate risks, the day to day management of the cost of living crisis will be managed at department levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Risks Removed
findings.headline: Asylum cost exposure reduced through hotel closure and tighter Home Office restrictions
findings.detail: The council's asylum risk has been downscaled following closure of one Leicestershire hotel, leaving only a smaller facility operational. The Home Office has introduced tighter restrictions on support for certain asylum seekers. Progress with community-based solutions to asylum dispersal has also strengthened the council's approach and resilience.
findings.matters: Asylum support is a significant unfunded cost pressure on councils; reduction in exposure improves the council's financial position
findings.figures: No specific financial figures provided in the paper
findings.quote: The risk score for asylum has been reduced. This change reflects the closure of one of the hotels in Leicestershire, which leaves only a smaller hotel in operation and therefore reduces the Council's overall exposure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC September Audit progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Leicestershire is scheduled for local government reorganisation with vesting day on 1 April 2028.
findings.detail: On 16 July 2026, the government announced that Leicestershire (together with Leicester and Rutland) will be replaced by a new unitary authority. Although a pause to LGR decisions was announced on 7 September 2026, the vesting date of 1 April 2028 remains scheduled, creating a 2-year transition period.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation creates structural uncertainty about governance, leadership, financial strategy and service continuity. The council's current corporate identity will be replaced in 2028, affecting continuity of relationships and risk profile.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028 vesting date; 134 existing councils nationally to be replaced by 38 new unitaries
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026 the government announced a pause to LGR decisions. For Leicestershire the Shadow Authority elections were due to take place in May 2027, with vesting day of new unitaries on 1 April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC September Audit progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit fees are expected to exceed the £289,960 baseline due to quality and timeliness issues.
findings.detail: PSAA published scale fees of £289,960 for the 2025-26 audit. The report explicitly states that additional fees may be charged due to poor quality working papers and delays in responses from the finance team, reflecting the need for additional auditor resources to deal with quality issues.
findings.matters: Audit cost inflation driven by quality issues is a proxy for operational weakness. It indicates the finance function is under resource or capability strain and reduces funds available for service delivery.
findings.figures: £289,960 baseline scale fee; additional fees TBD
findings.quote: Any additional fees required due to poor quality working papers or delays in response will be discussed and agreed with management and PSAA.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC September Audit progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit sample evidence quality is sub-standard across multiple high-risk areas.
findings.detail: Payables samples have 11 of 28 items missing required third-party supporting evidence (Amber rating). Grant income samples were not received by their due date of 17 August. Journals, fees and charges, and opex samples all show quality deficiencies or missing elements. The auditor has recommended the finance team enhance quality control procedures.
findings.matters: Weak audit evidence indicates internal control deficiencies in the finance function. This creates risk that the council's financial statements may not accurately reflect its financial position or that control weaknesses exist.
findings.figures: 11 of 28 payables items; grant income samples due 17 August not received as at 1 September 2026
findings.quote: It is recommended the finance team enhance its quality control procedures before evidence is provided to the audit team.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - LCC September Audit progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Leicestershire published financial statements on 30 June 2026, meeting the statutory deadline.
findings.detail: Financial statements were published in line with the national deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015, demonstrating timely compliance with statutory requirements. This achievement required effort from the Authority's staff.
findings.matters: Meeting statutory reporting deadlines demonstrates financial governance competence. Councils that miss these dates face enhanced scrutiny and potential borrowing cost implications.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026
findings.quote: The Authority published its financial statements on 30 June 2026, in line with the national deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015. We acknowledge the efforts made by the Authority's staff to ensure that this timetable was met.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Leicestershire Pension Fund - September Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: LGPS Central investments understated by £1.3bn in current-year related parties note; prior-year classification error being corrected
findings.detail: Auditors identified that the current-year related parties note (Note 25) understates LGPS Central investments by £1.3bn (£3.3bn reported vs £4.6bn correct as at 31 March 2026) and by £1.2bn in the prior-year comparative (£2.8bn vs £4bn). This follows identification and correction of a prior-year £1.123bn Legal & General investment that had been incorrectly classified as outside the LGPS Central pool. Management agreed to correct the Note 25 amounts.
findings.matters: Prior-year classification errors and current-year reporting inconsistencies indicate control weaknesses in investment accounting and raise questions about reliability of accounts and internal controls.
findings.figures: £1.123bn prior-year misclassification; £3.3bn vs £4.6bn variance (2025-26); £2.8bn vs £4bn variance (2024-25)
findings.quote: The related party note stated that as at 31 March 2026, £3.3bn of investments were managed by LGPS Central Limited (£2.8bn at 31st March 2025). These values need to be amended to £4.6bn as at 31 March 2026 and £4bn for the comparative period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Leicestershire Pension Fund - September Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £5.8m valuation understatement in Level 3 pension fund investments not being corrected, pending Committee approval
findings.detail: A timing lag in obtaining Level 3 investment valuations created a £5.8m factual understatement, with a further £1.1m extrapolated misstatement. Auditors do not identify this as a control weakness. Management proposes not to correct the factual understatement on grounds of immateriality; the Committee will be asked to confirm agreement through the Letter of Representation.
findings.matters: Unmodified errors in investment valuations indicate timing issues in accounting processes; the materiality judgment itself affects confidence in account accuracy.
findings.figures: £5.8m factual understatement; £1.1m extrapolated misstatement
findings.quote: This has been assessed as a factual understatement of £5.8m and further extrapolated misstatement of £1.1m Management are proposing not to amend the factual misstatement within the financial statements on the basis that the difference is not material both quantitatively and qualitatively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Leicestershire Pension Fund - September Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension fund audit opinion expected to be unmodified
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's fieldwork on the 2025-26 pension fund accounts is nearing completion with only minor procedures outstanding. No matters have been identified requiring modification of the audit opinion or material changes to the financial statements.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion confirms account reliability and is relevant to lender assessment of council financial position and governance.
findings.figures: Fieldwork June-August 2026
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit opinion will be unmodified.

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update - issue to CGC final
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation paused, leaving governance structure and resource allocation uncertain
findings.detail: The LGR process was paused pending government review shortly before this report. Implementation workstreams had been established but face unresolved risks including resource constraints conflicting with core service delivery, uncertain funding arrangements and unclear delivery timescales.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council stability needs to understand that governance restructuring has been halted with uncertain resumption, and that major programmes create resource conflicts affecting service delivery.
findings.figures: Pause announced before 2026-09-18; implementation was planned over extended period
findings.quote: there is a risk that LGR objectives and/or County Council priorities could be compromised if capacity pressures are not effectively managed

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Update - issue to CGC final
findings.headline: SEND services expansion depends on capital investment that may not be available
findings.detail: The council has redefined its SEND risk to explicitly identify capital investment as a constraint on meeting statutory responsibilities. The risk now encompasses demand for assessments, reviews, specialist placements, alternative provision and school places. Without sufficient capital to deliver additional provision, the council may be unable to meet statutory SEND obligations.
findings.matters: Flagging that capital constraints could prevent delivery of statutory services indicates unmet infrastructure needs and potential for service pressures or reserve depletion to bridge the gap.

findings.quote: if sufficient capital investment is not available to deliver the required additional places, specialist and alternative provision, then the Council may be unable to meet its statutory responsibilities for SEND and place planning

findings.paper_title: CGC180926 - Audit Progress Report SOA
findings.headline: A £5.8 million underestimate of hard-to-value asset valuations was identified in the Pension Fund audit
findings.detail: An underestimation in Level 3 valuation hierarchy assets (unquoted private equity, private debt, and pooled investments) totals £5.8m, rising to £1.1m when extrapolated across all relevant investments. The auditor has determined this is immaterial against the £93.6m materiality threshold, and no adjustment to the Pension Fund financial statements is required.

findings.quote: One immaterial item has been identified relating to an under estimation of the valuation of hard to value assets, those meeting the level 3 valuation hierarchy. The underestimate totals £5.8m which increases by a further £1.1m when extrapolated for all relevant investments.

findings.paper_title: CGC180926 - Audit Progress Report SOA
findings.headline: The council's prior year accounts received an unmodified audit opinion and draft 2025/26 statements met the statutory publication deadline
findings.detail: The 2024/25 financial statements were signed on time with an unmodified audit opinion (meaning no qualification of the accounts). Draft 2025/26 financial statements were published by the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline. The current audit is expected to complete by end of November 2026, well ahead of the 31 January 2027 statutory backstop.
findings.matters: Timely, unqualified financial statements are fundamental to a lender's assessment of the council's financial controls and governance quality.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Economic Overview (Jun 2026)
findings.headline: Bank of England rates expected to remain at 3.75% through 2026, with upside risk, but 10-year gilt yields remain volatile between 4.7% and 5.18%.
findings.detail: Bank rate held at 3.75% through Q2 2026 despite two MPC members voting for a 0.25% rise in June. The briefing expects rates to stay at 3.75% for the remainder of 2026. However, 10-year gilt yields moved from 5.18% (highest since 2008) in mid-May to 4.76% by end of quarter. PWLB rates, which councils access for borrowing, track gilt yields, so this volatility directly affects refinancing costs.
findings.matters: If the council has debt maturing in 2026/27, refinancing will occur at rates significantly elevated from historical norms. Even at the lower end (4.7%), long-term borrowing costs are roughly 100 basis points above pre-2022 rates.

findings.quote: the 10-year Gilt shot up to 5.18% in mid-May, its highest level since 2008. While that largely reflects the surge in energy prices, sticky domestic inflation concerns and a rising UK political risk premium also put some upward pressure on the yield at the margin. Since, positive developments in the US-Iran conflict has led to a fall in oil and gas prices. The 10-year Gilt yield has generally traced that move, falling back to 4.7% in June.

findings.matters: Inflation expectations affect the council's operating costs (energy bills for council buildings, transport costs, contract inflation). At 3.6%, the council's input costs will rise faster than council tax (typically capped at ~2% annual increases).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Economic Overview (Jun 2026)
findings.headline: Government borrowing is now forecast to rise to 4.4% of GDP in 2026/27, materially above the March forecast of 3.6%.

findings.matters: Deteriorating government finances signal tightening fiscal constraints across the public sector. A lender assesses whether central government funding to councils will remain available or be cut; a finance director needs to plan assuming reduced government support.

findings.paper_title: FINAL MTFS Sept 26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Of £23m savings targeted for 2026/27, £0.6m is projected to fall short and £3.9m (ten initiatives) have delivery concerns; Better Leicestershire Programme's £27m identified savings not yet built into MTFS

Savings shortfalls lead to larger-than-forecast deficits, faster reserve depletion, and service cuts. This signals execution risk in the council's financial recovery plan.

findings.detail: Multiple cost drivers are pressuring the adult social care budget. Supported living shows a £1.3m overspend driven by a sharp increase in average hours per service user (+4%) observed in Q4 2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27, plus very high-needs packages above average cost. Direct Cash Payments show a £1.2m overspend (shortfall on clawbacks £0.5m, higher average package costs £0.7m). Better Care Fund income is £1.2m down due to lower activity on discharge-to-assess income (£1.6m forecast vs £2.8m budget). Service user numbers in homecare rose 2.85% between February and May 2026 (2,730 to 2,813), with historic data suggesting further increases expected in autumn as young adults transition from children's services.
findings.matters: Adult social care is one of the largest council budgets with demand-led costs outside council control. Sustained growth in service user numbers, increased hours per user, and escalating average package costs signal structural cost growth that will persist. These are key indicators of sustained financial pressure on council resources.
findings.figures: Supported living £1.3m overspend; Direct Cash Payments £1.2m overspend; Better Care Fund £1.2m overspend; Homecare service users 2,730→2,813 (+2.85%) Feb-May 2026; average hours 10.8 per user
findings.quote: The overspend reflects a sharp increase in the average hours per service user (+4%) that was observed in the final quarter of 2025/26 that is expected to continue into 2026/27. findings.paper_title: FINAL MTFS Sept 26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Around ten schools likely to require additional funding for expansion, with council unable to fund shortfalls and describing position as 'significant Education and financial risk'
findings.detail: The council has committed discretionary revenue funding to cover school place provision shortfalls: £12.6m in summer 2025 and £6.7m in February 2026. A further ten schools are likely to require additional funding in the new MTFS. Shortfalls are caused by construction cost inflation outpacing developer contribution indexation, new requirements (zero-carbon, sprinkler systems) not anticipated in legacy Section 106 agreements, and cuts to DfE Basic Need capital funding following the DfE's change to funding methodology (which now applies minimum place thresholds and discounts pupils from housing developments). Recent schemes have experienced cost overruns from planning delays and additional conditions.
findings.matters: The council is diverting revenue to cover capital project shortfalls that should be funded from government grant or developer contributions. This diverts resources from core service delivery and signals an inability to fund essential infrastructure from standard sources. Repeated cost escalation and unfunded requirements indicate delivery risk.
findings.figures: £12.6m discretionary funding summer 2025; £6.7m February 2026; around ten additional schools requiring funding in new MTFS
findings.quote: There are around a further ten schools that are likely to require additional funding in the new MTFS. The department is urgently reviewing the position and options to reduce the costs and funding shortfalls. However, this remains a significant Education and financial risk to the Council.

findings.paper_title: FINAL MTFS Sept 26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Revenue budget balanced only through use of £10.6m from reserves in 2026/27, following £6m in 2024/25 and £5m in 2025/26, with projected medium-term funding gaps of £34m rising to £85m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council required £15m from reserves to balance the initial 2026/27 budget (reduced to £10.6m through in-year underspend), perpetuating a three-year pattern of reserve depletion (£6m in 2024/25, £5m in 2025/26). The original MTFS forecast funding gaps of £34m in 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30 despite £115m savings being targeted and £313m already delivered since 2010. The report warns explicitly that 'ongoing reliance on reserves to balance the budget should be avoided' because reserves 'can only be used once' and this approach 'does not solve the structural imbalance between income and expenditure that inflation and spending pressures are causing.'
findings.matters: Systematic depletion of reserves to cover recurring deficits signals the council cannot sustainably fund services from taxation and government grant. This is a key credit indicator—once reserves are exhausted, the council must choose between cutting services, raising tax significantly, or borrowing, all constrained options that affect lender security.
findings.figures: £15m→£10.6m from reserves 2026/27; £6m 2024/25; £5m 2025/26; £115m savings targeted in current MTFS; £313m already delivered since 2010; £34m funding gap 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30
findings.quote: To balance the budget the use of reserves or other short-term measures may need to be considered as was the case with the County Council's 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27 budgets, with £6m, £5m and £15m respectively being required from reserves to balance the initial budgets. Reserves can only be used once and ongoing reliance on reserves to balance the budget should be avoided.

findings.paper_title: FINAL MTFS Sept 26 Cabinet
findings.headline: High Needs Block overspend of £62.2m in 2026/27, with cumulative DSG deficit of £79.2m and projected growth to £400m by March 2030 before government support
findings.detail: The council faces a chronic SEND funding crisis. The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit at end of 2025/26 was £79.2m, driven by sustained growth in funded Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs). Active EHCPs reached 8,786 at January 2026 (193% increase since 2016) and 9,188 by mid-July 2026. The paper states that if demand continues on similar trajectory, the deficit could reach £400m by March 2030. Government support covers only 90% of deficits as at March 2026; no confirmation yet of support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits. The paper explicitly describes this position as 'unsustainable.'
findings.matters: A £79m accumulated liability growing by demand pressures outside the council's control, with only partial government cover confirmed and a potential four-year trajectory to £400m, represents a material unfunded obligation that constrains financial flexibility and credit quality.
findings.figures: £62.2m High Needs overspend 2026/27; £79.2m cumulative DSG deficit at end 2025/26; projected £400m by March 2030; 8,786 active EHCPs at January 2026 (193% increase since 2016); 9,188 EHCPs mid-July 2026 (5% increase in first half calendar year); government support covers 90% of March 2026 deficit only

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Council maintains £388m cash balance and is £63m under-borrowed, using internal funding instead of market borrowing for capital investment
findings.detail: Leicestershire holds £387.5m in short-term investments and £388m total cash balance as at 31 March 2026. The Council is £63m under-borrowed relative to its Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), internally funding this gap from cash reserves rather than raising external debt. This is cost-effective in current conditions (investment returns ~4% vs 6%+ cost of long-term borrowing) and provides headroom, but sustainability depends on disciplined capital spending and cash management.
findings.matters: Strong liquidity buffers creditors, but large cash balances tied to internal borrowing represent opportunity cost and depletion risk as capital programmes accelerate and base rates fall

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: UK gilt yields at 20+ year highs are making external borrowing expensive; council funds capital programme from internal reserves instead of market access
findings.detail: UK gilt yields have risen to their highest levels this century as at end of 2025/26 and into May 2026. These yields underpin PWLB rates and determine the cost of external borrowing. In response, the Council's capital programme (£65m requirement 2026-2030) is planned to be funded from internal balances rather than market borrowing. This pattern has been consistent since August 2010, when the Council last raised new external loans.
findings.matters: Rising gilt yields increase refinancing risk and explain 16 years without market access; the strategy is only viable while internal cash balances remain strong, and poses refinancing risk if capital spending needs accelerate beyond cash generation
findings.figures: Gilt yields at 20+ year highs, PWLB average rate on remaining debt 5.54%, £65m capital programme 2026-2030, no external borrowing since August 2010
findings.quote: Moreover, borrowing has become more expensive in 2025/26. UK gilt yields have risen materially by year end, and into May 2026 to their highest yields this century.
